title: A Generalizable Machine Learning Framework for Half-Heusler Thermoelectrics
summary: Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful approach for accelerating the discovery of thermoelectric (TE) materials, yet many models suffer from limited generalizability. Here we present a robust ML framework for predicting the thermoelectric figure of merit (zT) in half-Heusler (hH) compounds, emphasizing prediction of previously unseen compositions. A principal component analysis (PCA)-based train/test splitting strategy is introduced to generate representative partitions of chemical space. Bayesian hyperparameter optimization is combined with correlation-based k-best feature selection for Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models, together with the interpretable SISSO symbolic-regression method. Relative to the full set of 118 input features, the optimized feature subsets reduce the test RMSE by 16-27%. SHAP and SISSO analyses identify temperature, A-site dopant concentration, and A-site heat of vaporization as the most important descriptors of zT. The framework is validated through prediction of previously unexplored compositions, recovery of literature-reported optimal zT values for established hH systems, and first-principles calculations for the new compounds CeCoBi and CeIrBi, which exhibit favorable electronic transport properties. The framework is further applied to high-throughput screening of the doped hH chemical space, covering about 2.46 million elemental substitution combinations across 631 thermodynamically screened parent matrices under stability constraints. This screening yields a concise set of promising candidates for future study. Overall, the work establishes a generalizable workflow for reliable data-driven thermoelectric materials discovery.

title: An introduction to local differential privacy protocols using block designs
comments: Theorem 3.6 has been corrected and various other changes have been made
summary:
The design of protocols for local differential privacy (or LDP) has been a topic of considerable research interest in recent years. LDP protocols utilise the randomised encoding of outcomes of an experiment using a transition probability matrix (TPM). Several authors have observed that balanced incomplete block designs (BIBDs) provide nice examples of TPMs for LDP protocols. Indeed, it has been shown that such BIBD-based LDP protocols provide optimal estimators.
  In this primarily expository paper, we give a detailed introduction to LDP protocols and their connections with block designs. We prove that a subclass of LDP protocols known as pure LDP protocols are equivalent to $(r,λ)$-designs (which contain balanced incomplete block designs as a special case). An unbiased estimator for an LDP scheme is a left inverse of the transition probability matrix. We show that the optimal estimators for BIBD-based TPMs are precisely those obtained from the Moore-Penrose inverse of the corresponding TPM. We also review some existing work on optimal LDP protocols in the context of pure protocols.
comment: Theorem 3.6 has been corrected and various other changes have been made

title: Fast Rates for Nonstationary Weighted Risk Minimization
summary: Weighted empirical risk minimization is a common approach to prediction under distribution drift. This article studies its out-of-sample prediction error under nonstationarity. We provide a general decomposition of the excess risk into a learning term and an error term associated with distribution drift, and prove oracle inequalities for the learning error under mixing conditions. The learning bound holds uniformly over arbitrary weight classes and accounts for the effective sample size induced by the weight vector, the complexity of the weight and hypothesis classes, and potential data dependence. We also analyze the drift error in the square loss setting and provide explicit bounds for structural-break and smoothly drifting processes. We then combine the learning and drift analysis in (auto-) regression problems with linear models, basis approximations, and neural networks. In all cases, the optimal weights are characterized by a bias--variance trade-off between learning and drift, while minimax-optimal rates (up to logarithmic factors) are recovered when specialized to unweighted and stationary settings.

title: RanSOM: Second-Order Momentum with Randomized Scaling for Constrained and Unconstrained Optimization
summary: Second-order momentum corrects the lag of momentum behind the current gradient with a Hessian-vector product (HVP), but existing corrections need either a Lipschitz Hessian or extra forward and backward passes at an auxiliary point. We show that randomizing the step length removes this trade-off: if the step is exponentially distributed with mean $η$, a Stein-type identity makes $η$ times one HVP at the new iterate an estimate of the gradient change that is unbiased in expectation over the step, and this HVP shares its forward pass with the next gradient. The resulting method, RanSOM-E, works with normalized, sign, and Muon-type steps, and a Beta-distributed variant, RanSOM-B, keeps Frank-Wolfe iterates feasible. For objectives with Lipschitz gradient and heavy-tailed gradient and Hessian noise with tail indices $p, q \in (1,2]$, RanSOM-E attains the optimal oracle-complexity exponents for every pair $(p,q)$, including $p \neq q$, without a Lipschitz Hessian or clipping ($\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ for $p = q = 2$). On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20, we detect no accuracy difference from existing second-order momentum methods, and its mean update time is lower than that of the auxiliary-point method.

title: Coherent Information Deletion: Bayesian, Generalized Bayesian and Possibilistic Unlearning
comments: Extended the deletion rule to generalized Bayes and Possibilistic inference
summary: Bayes' theorem admits an information processing interpretation due to Zellner (1988): under the Shannon information criterion, the posterior is the unique rule that processes prior and data information without information loss. We revisit these ideas from the perspective of information deletion. Given a posterior based on a complete dataset, what distribution should replace it when a subset of the data is removed? For ordinary Bayesian inference, we show that the corresponding information deletion objective is uniquely minimized by the leave-data-out posterior. We then extend the framework beyond likelihood-based inference from Bayes to the generalized Bayesian updating of Bissiri et al.(2016} based on loss functions. Requiring deletion to be coherent under sequential removal of loss contributions yields a deletion rule that exactly recovers the generalized posterior based only on the retained information. We further develop an axiomatic theory, beyond probabilistic inference, for possibilistic deletion and show that the same information-deletion perspective leads to a principled rule for exact possibilistic unlearning. Finally, restricting these exact deletion principles to tractable families leads naturally to variational Bayesian, generalized Bayesian, and maxitive possibilistic unlearning.
comment: Extended the deletion rule to generalized Bayes and Possibilistic inference

title: Locally Private Parametric Methods for Change-Point Detection
summary: We study parametric change-point detection under local differential privacy, focusing on the offline localization of a single change point in a sequence of independent observations.~In the non-private setting, we derive improved finite-sample accuracy guarantees for a generalized likelihood-ratio estimator using martingale methods.~We establish finite-sample minimax lower bounds in both the non-private and locally private settings, showing that localization accuracy is fundamentally limited by the Chernoff information between the pre- and post-change distributions.~Guided by this, we design locally private CPD algorithms based on aggregated randomized response and binary mechanisms, which maximize the Chernoff information between the induced output distributions in low- and high-privacy regimes, respectively, and derive their finite-sample guarantees. Together, our upper and lower bounds quantify the statistical cost of privacy in change-point localization.~As part of our analysis, we also show that strong data processing inequality coefficients of Rényi divergence and Jeffreys--Rényi divergence of order infinity can be computed by restricting to pairs of input distributions with a common support of at most two symbols.~We corroborate our results through empirical evaluation on synthetic data.

title: The Smallest String Attractors of Fibonacci, Period-Doubling, and Thue--Morse Words
comments: Extended version of CPM 2026 paper, adding full characterization of the smallest attractors of Thue-Morse words, and details of the verification of results using the Walnut theorem prover
summary: A string attractor of a string $T[1..|T|]$ is a set of positions $Γ$ of $T$ such that any nonempty substring $w$ of $T$ has an occurrence that crosses a position in $Γ$, i.e., there is a position $i$ such that $w = T[i..i+|w|-1]$ and the intersection $[i,i+|w|-1]\cap Γ$ is nonempty. The size of the smallest string attractor of Fibonacci words and period-doubling words of length at least $2$ is known to be $2$. The size of the smallest string attractor of Thue--Morse words of length at least $25$ is known to be $4$. We completely characterize the set of all smallest string attractors of Fibonacci words, period-doubling words, and Thue--Morse words. For Fibonacci words, we show a recursive formula describing the $2^{n-4} + 2^{\lceil n/2 \rceil - 2}$ distinct position pairs that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th Fibonacci word for $n \geq 7$. For period-doubling words, we show a formula describing the two distinct position pairs that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th period-doubling word for $n\geq 2$. For Thue--Morse words, we show a formula describing the 32 sets of four positions that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th Thue--Morse word for $n\geq 6$. Our results show that strings with the same smallest attractor size can have a drastically different number of distinct smallest attractors.
comment: Extended version of CPM 2026 paper, adding full characterization of the smallest attractors of Thue-Morse words, and details of the verification of results using the Walnut theorem prover

title: A Multi-Scenario UAV RF Dataset with Real-World Acquisition and Signal Processing Benchmarking
summary: We present a real-world multi-scenario unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) radio frequency (RF) dataset, namely DRFF-R2, which is collected using a dedicated acquisition platform under diverse operational conditions. All signals are acquired within a unified framework to ensure consistency in hardware configuration and environmental settings. The dataset is systematically organized into seven well-defined subsets corresponding to different operational and signal composition scenarios to facilitate structured experimentation. Each file follows a clearly annotated naming convention to enable convenient data indexing and reproducible analysis. The dataset contains RF recordings from 26 UAV units spanning 8 distinct models, captured across varying flight states, altitudes, speeds, acquisition days, and receiver configurations. By covering diverse acquisition settings and signal compositions, the dataset provides a comprehensive resource for future UAV RF signal research, including RF fingerprinting (RFF) identification, model-level recognition, flight state analysis, time-varying RFF study, and interference-aware signal processing.

title: Featurized Occupation Measures for Structured Global Search in Numerical Optimal Control
summary: Numerical optimal control is split between globally structured but dimensionally intractable Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) methods and scalable but local trajectory optimization. We introduce Featurized Occupation Measures (FOM), a finite-dimensional primal--dual interface where HJB subsolutions guide primal search and primal occupation data can inform certificate refinement. Explicit and implicit realizations, based on finite Liouville tests and rollout-sampled residuals, are proved asymptotically consistent with the exact occupation-measure LP. FOM also identifies when HJB-type certificates avoid full state-space representation. For factor graphs induced by compatible passivity-based interconnections, blockwise HJB inequalities yield block-additive OM-dual certificates, including blockwise approximate variants. The curse of dimensionality is then shifted from state dimension to interconnection topology. Approximate certificates remain reusable under time shifts and bounded model perturbations, with explicit degradation bounds. A static obstacle-avoidance benchmark illustrates how tighter certificates improve sample-based global search.

title: Exact analytical PGSE signal for diffusion confined to a cylindrical surface using a spectral Laplacian formalism
summary: Objective. To derive an exact analytical expression for the diffusion MRI signal arising from diffusion confined to a cylindrical surface under finite rectangular pulsed-gradient spin-echo (PGSE) gradients, and to develop computationally efficient strategies for repeated model evaluations. Approach. The Bloch-Torrey equation was solved using a spectral matrix formalism of the Laplace operator in the eigenbasis of the cylindrical surface. The resulting signal is expressed as a product of non-commuting matrix exponentials and is valid for arbitrary rectangular gradient durations and separations, without approximations to the diffusion propagator or spin phase distribution. A reduced real spectral basis was introduced to decrease the dimensionality of the problem. Accelerated implementations based on Strang splitting and Gauss-Legendre quadrature were developed for repeated signal evaluations and computation of the spherical mean. The analytical signal was validated against Monte Carlo diffusion simulations. Main results. The exact formulation showed excellent agreement with Monte Carlo simulations over a wide range of cylinder radii and acquisition parameters. The spectral expansion converged rapidly with mode order, and the reduced basis substantially decreased computational cost without loss of accuracy. The accelerated implementations provided large additional speed-ups while retaining controllable errors relative to the exact solution. Significance. The proposed framework extends exact finite-pulse solutions of the Bloch-Torrey equation to diffusion confined to cylindrical surfaces and provides practical implementations for directional and orientationally averaged diffusion MRI signals. It therefore offers an approximation-free reference for assessing faster signal approximations and for applications requiring large numbers of model evaluations.

title: Optimizing Entanglement Distribution Protocols: Maximizing Classical Information in Quantum Networks
summary: Large-scale quantum networks depend on the efficient distribution of entangled pairs between distant nodes. However, state-of-the-art solutions rely on restrictive operational assumptions, incur prohibitive computational complexity, and optimize metrics misaligned with application needs. This paper addresses the entanglement distribution problem introducing four pivotal advances. First, since the primary application of quantum communication is private information transmission, we derive the Ensemble Capacity, a novel metric that quantifies the private classical information enabled by entanglement distribution. Second, we propose a generalized formulation of the Entanglement Distribution Problem that allows arbitrary sequencing of entanglement swapping and purification, removing the structural restrictions of prior models. Third, to navigate the resulting combinatorial space, we introduce a dynamic programming-based hypergraph generation algorithm that preserves exact, continuous fidelities, avoiding quantization, while pruning sub-optimal sequences in advance. Finally, we integrate these solutions into CODE, a two-tier orchestration framework enabling near-real-time network operation. Extensive evaluations show that our approach achieves higher private information capacity and significantly lower computational complexity than existing solutions, while meeting the sub-second latency requirements of dynamic quantum network operation.

title: Rethinking Entropy Allocation in LLM-based ASR: Understanding the Dynamics between Speech Encoders and LLMs
summary: Integrating large language models (LLMs) into automatic speech recognition (ASR) has become a dominant paradigm. Although recent LLM-based ASR models have shown promising performance on public benchmarks, it remains challenging to balance recognition quality with latency and overhead, while hallucinations further limit real-world deployment. In this study, we revisit LLM-based ASR from an entropy allocation perspective and introduce three metrics to characterize how training paradigms allocate entropy reduction between the speech encoder and the LLM. To remedy entropy-allocation inefficiencies in prevailing approaches, we propose a principled multi-stage training strategy grounded in capability-boundary awareness, optimizing parameter efficiency and hallucination robustness. Specifically, we redesign the pretraining strategy to alleviate the speech-text modality gap, and further introduce an iterative asynchronous SFT stage between alignment and joint SFT to preserve functional decoupling and constrain encoder representation drift. Experiments on Mandarin and English benchmarks show that our method achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art models using only 2.3B parameters, while also effectively mitigating hallucinations through our decoupling-oriented design.

title: Physics-guided surrogate learning enables zero-shot control of turbulent wings
summary: Turbulent boundary layers over aerodynamic surfaces are a major source of aircraft drag, yet their control remains challenging due to multiscale dynamics and spatial variability, particularly under adverse pressure gradients. Reinforcement learning has outperformed state-of-the-art strategies in canonical flows, but its application to realistic geometries is limited by computational cost and transferability. Here we show that these limitations can be overcome by exploiting local structures of wall-bounded turbulence. Policies are trained in turbulent channel flows matched to wing boundary-layer statistics and deployed directly onto a NACA4412 wing section at $Re_c=2\times10^5$ without additional training on the wing, constituting zero-shot deployment. The transferred policies reduce total drag by 11.1\%, while state-of-the-art opposition control reduces it by 8.9\%. With the actuation cost taken into account, the corresponding net-energy savings are 10.9\% and 8.8\%, respectively. Surrogate training provides an estimated improvement of four orders of magnitude in exploration efficiency over direct on-wing training, enabling scalable flow control.

title: Selective Depthwise Separable Convolution for Lightweight Joint Source-Channel Coding in Wireless Image Transmission
summary: Depthwise separable convolutional (DSConv) layers have been successfully applied to deep learning (DL)-based joint source-channel coding (JSCC) schemes to reduce computational complexity. However, a systematic investigation of the layerwise and ratio-wise replacement of standard convolutional (Conv) layers with DSConv layers in JSCC systems for wireless image transmission remains largely unexplored. In this letter, we propose a configurable lightweight JSCC framework that incorporates a selective replacement strategy, enabling flexible Conv-to-DSConv replacement at different replacement ratios and positions. By varying the replacement ratio, we obtain models with different computational complexities and analyze their impact on reconstruction performance. Furthermore, we investigate how replacements at different encoder and decoder depths influence reconstruction quality under a fixed replacement ratio. Our results show that Conv-to-DSConv replacement at the intermediate layers of the encoder and decoder achieves a favorable complexity-performance trade-off, revealing layer-wise redundancy in DL-based JSCC systems. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves substantial parameter reduction with only slight performance degradation, enabling flexible complexity-performance trade-offs for resource-constrained edge devices.

title: Occam's Razor is Only as Sharp as Your ELBO
summary: The marginal likelihood, also known as the evidence, is regarded as a mathematical embodiment of Occam's razor, enabling hyperparameter selection that avoids overfitting. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) objective from variational inference has also been used for similar purposes. In this paper, we define a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for Bayesian linear regression in terms of key hyperparameters controlling signal and noise variance. We then study how ELBO-based hyperparameter learning can under or overestimate SNR depending on the assumed covariance matrix structure in a Gaussian approximate posterior. We prove that assuming a diagonal or low-rank plus diagonal covariance matrix underestimates the SNR, while a low-rank covariance matrix overestimates the SNR. Underestimating the SNR leads to higher than optimal mean squared error on the training set (underfitting), while overestimating SNR leads to lower error (overfitting). Bayesian practitioners hoping to scale to large models should be cautious about how covariance assumptions needed for tractability may impact model selection.

title: Stochastic Compositional Optimization via Hybrid Momentum Frank--Wolfe
summary: Stochastic compositional optimization minimizes $F(f(x), x)$ over a compact convex set when the inner map $f$ is available only through noisy samples. We propose Hybrid Momentum Stochastic Frank--Wolfe, a projection-free method for outer functions $F$ that are jointly convex and Lipschitz but not necessarily differentiable, such as maxima, CVaR, and norms. The method tracks the Jacobian and the value of $f$ with momentum, using a Taylor correction for the value, and passes the tracked linearization to a generalized linear minimization oracle. Under finite-variance noise, it attains an expected generalized Frank--Wolfe gap of order $K^{-1/4}$ for non-convex objectives and, when the linearized models minorize the objective, a last-iterate primal error of order $K^{-1/3}$. The analysis extends to heavy-tailed noise without clipping, with separate moment orders for values and Jacobians. With an exact oracle, the method reduces to the deterministic method of Vladarean et al. (2023).

title: Cross-View Attention Fusion Net: A Prior-Guided Dual-View Representation Learning for Cardiac Output Estimation from Short-Term PPG Signals
summary: Accurate cardiac output (CO) estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) is promising for unobtrusive hemodynamic monitoring, but remains difficult since CO is jointly determined by cardiac function and vascular tone. Conventional feature-based models use physiologically meaningful PPG descriptors, yet depend on accurate pulse detection and may miss latent temporal relationships. In contrast, fully end-to-end deep learning models learn directly from raw PPG but often underuse established PPG-derived prior information. Here, we introduce the Cross-View Attention Fusion Network (CVAF-Net), a prior-guided dual-view deep learning model for CO estimation from short, fixed-length PPG segments. CVAF-Net processes raw PPG as a temporal view and a feature sequence map (FSM) as a structured prior-guided view, and fuses the two representations through cross-view attention. The model was independently evaluated using 5-, 15-, and 30-s segments from three datasets: simulated pulse waves (3323 subjects), vasoconstriction provocation (79 subjects), and resting/cycling activities (10 subjects), and was compared with multiple machine learning and deep learning benchmarks. CVAF-Net outperformed most benchmark methods and achieved performance comparable to a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.19 L/min (MAPE: 3.95%) on simulated data and high accuracy in real-world settings (minimum MAE: 1.20 L/min). Importantly, CVAF-Net reduced FLOPs by twelvefold compared with the leading Transformer-based model. Plausibility analysis showed physiologically consistent CO estimates, with expected correlations with age ($ρ= -0.274$), heart rate ($ρ= 0.894$), and systemic vascular resistance ($ρ= -0.740$). These findings indicate that CVAF-Net provides an accurate, computationally efficient, and generalizable approach for continuous wearable-based CO monitoring.

title: Is TabPFN the Silver Bullet for Insurance Pricing?
summary: Modelling claim frequency and severity for non-life insurance pricing predominantly relies on generalised linear models (GLMs), with gradient-boosted machines as the leading machine learning alternative. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) present a fundamentally different inference paradigm. By pre-training on large collections of synthetic datasets, TFMs enable inference on new data through in-context learning, without any dataset-specific preprocessing, fitting, or hyperparameter tuning. This paper presents a first empirical evaluation of TabPFN for motor insurance pricing, benchmarking two versions of TabPFN against GLM and XGBoost on two publicly available motor third-party liability (MTPL) datasets. Our results show that TabPFN does not consistently outperform established baselines: it falls behind the GLM on claim frequency, where its performance depends on the size of the in-context training set, but it is competitive on claim severity, where data are scarcer. Its inference times are substantially longer. Although tabular foundation models are promising, particularly in data-scarce settings, TabPFN is not yet ready to replace established actuarial methods for claim frequency.

title: Unsupervised Identification and Removal of Spurious Correlations During Fine-Tuning
summary: Fine-tuning a pretrained language model on a curated dataset can produce spurious correlations between the fine-tuning task and unintended latent factors---such as misaligned personas or political slant---that the curation procedure has entangled with the task. The model can latch onto these spurious correlations, leading to bias and reduced out-of-distribution generalisation. We prove that under reasonable assumptions on task complexity and the spurious correlation, such latent factors can be identified, without supervision, from the weights of a naive LoRA fine-tune. Existing approaches to removing bias, such as activation steering, remove identified factors from residual-stream activations, either at inference or during training. We argue, however, that the goal should be to remove the spurious correlation, not the latent factor itself, as the pretrained model may rely on it for genuine task signal. To enable this, we propose GRASP, GRadient projection of Associated Spurious Patterns, which prevents the model from acquiring new reliance on the identified latent factor while preserving any pretrained content along it. We validate on three fine-tuning tasks. The first two involve emergent misalignment, where fine-tuning on a narrow task---in our case, writing insecure code and giving bad medical advice---leads to misaligned responses on unrelated topics. Here our method completely removes misalignment in the insecure code case and reduces it by ~5x in the bad medical advice case, beating all baselines in the trade-off between misalignment-reduction and task-preservation. The last is a novel political-bias experiment, where fine-tuning on right-skewed Reddit financial-advice data causes political-lean drift on unrelated topics. Here our method reduces drift by more than half, while improving financial task performance, beating all baselines.

title: Automatic-Differentiation-Enabled Finite Element Model Updating: Learning Constitutive Neural Networks from Structural Deformation Data
summary: The identification of constitutive neural network models from heterogeneous full-field deformation data provides a robust alternative to traditional calibration methods based on homogeneous stress-strain experiments, particularly given the high dimensionality of trainable parameters. This work presents ADE-FEMU (Automatic-Differentiation-Enabled Finite Element Model Updating), an end-to-end differentiable framework that integrates a constitutive neural network model within a JAX-FEM nonlinear solver and identifies its parameters through gradient-based minimization of a measurement-mismatch loss, allowing for training on structural data with limited kinetic information. Thus, it can be considered as an extension of finite element model updating (FEMU) for hyperelastic materials, implemented within a GPU-accelerated, fully automatically differentiable finite element framework Newton tangent stiffness and loss gradients are computed automatically using forward- and reverse-mode automatic differentiation throughout the entire pipeline, thereby removing the need for analytic adjoints or offline surrogate models. ADE-FEMU is demonstrated for two architectures: a grey-box Constitutive Artificial Neural Network (CANN), a polyconvex, fully connected model with high flexibility, and a white-box CANN, an expert-system network with phenomenologically interpretable strain-energy terms. Focusing on incompressible isotropic hyperelasticity, ADE-FEMU is evaluated on three open experimental datasets: (1) full digital image correlation (DIC) of a perforated tensile specimen, (2) a reduced-data scenario with a one-dimensional stretch profile and global force-displacement curve, and (3) a heterogeneous matrix-inclusion system in which both phases constitutive laws are identified and generalized to twenty-two previously unseen samples.

title: Hamilton paths and cycles in flip graphs of (almost-)perfect matchings
summary: We consider the set of matchings of a graph and a local change operation, called a flip, between them. In the combinatorial setting, the base graphs are either complete graphs or complete bipartite graphs, and in the geometric setting, the graphs are embedded on point sets in the plane, with the requirement that edges must be drawn as straight lines and must not cross. For base graphs with an even number of vertices, we consider perfect matchings, i.e., all vertices are matched, and for base graphs with an odd number of vertices, we consider almost-perfect matchings, i.e., all but one vertex of the graph are matched. A 2-flip between two perfect matchings exchanges two edges, and a 1-flip between two almost-perfect matchings exchanges one edge. The corresponding flip graph has the set of perfect or almost-perfect matchings as vertices, with pairs of them connected by an edge if they differ in a 2-flip or 1-flip, respectively. In this work, we provide a comprehensive picture of Hamiltonicity properties of these flip graphs. We prove that the flip graphs in the combinatorial setting are Hamilton-connected, i.e., they admit a Hamilton path between any two vertices, or, if the flip graphs are bipartite, we prove that they are Hamilton-laceable, i.e., they admit a Hamilton path between any two vertices from different partition classes. In the geometric setting, we prove that any path in them misses exponentially many vertices, in particular, they have no Hamilton paths or cycles. For points in convex position and almost-perfect matchings under 1-flips, we complement this by constructing a cycle in the flip graph that visits almost all vertices.

title: Equality, Equity, and Causality in Fairness Research: A Commentary on Cheng (2026)
comments: Invited commentary on Cheng (2026), doi:10.1017/psy.2026.10110; accepted in Psychometrika
summary: This is an invited commentary on the Psychometrika focus article "Fairness Issues and Evaluation in Psychometrics and AI/ML: What Can We Learn from Each Field?" by Ying Cheng (2026, doi:10.1017/psy.2026.10110). Cheng offers a systematic comparison between long-standing test fairness and modern algorithmic fairness. Her mapping of the entire testing workflow onto the AI/ML fairness paradigm, rather than only the final selection stage, is a crucial contribution to interdisciplinary fairness research. This commentary extends her discussion by examining two conceptual issues: the distinction between equality and equity, and the role of causality in fairness research. The focus article and this commentary point to directions for future fairness research across the psychometrics and AI/ML communities.
comment: Invited commentary on Cheng (2026), doi:10.1017/psy.2026.10110; accepted in Psychometrika

title: Particle-based Generalised Stochastic Optimisation
summary: We develop a class of general diffusion-based stochastic particle optimisation methods for loss functions with intractable gradients. Specifically, we consider problems in which the loss gradient is an integral with respect to a parameter-dependent distribution, a structure that includes training generative models, fine-tuning, and learning latent-variable models. We introduce mean-field dynamics and its interacting-particle approximations, which contain several existing algorithms as special cases and provide a route to constructing new methods. Under well-posedness and joint contractivity assumptions, we prove exponential convergence and show that the continuous-time particle system admits a non-asymptotic error bound. We illustrate our framework by developing higher-order Langevin and momentum optimisers and evaluating them on maximum marginal-likelihood estimation and energy-based-model training.

title: Nonsmooth Optimization via Orthogonalized Momentum
summary: Modern real application problems involve matrix-valued parameters, yet conventional optimizers treat them as vectors, thereby motivating matrix-aware methods that exploit input-output geometry, such as Muon which orthogonalizes the momentum matrices before parameter updates. Its empirical success raises a conceptual question: can orthogonalized momentum remain effective beyond smooth optimization? This paper studies this question for locally Lipschitz functions using a generalized derivative framework compatible with backpropagation. Our first contribution is to identify a key limitation: for every fixed momentum factor $β\in[0,1)$, Muon can fail to approach the global optimal solution of a convex Lipschitz objective from almost every initialization, when step sizes adapt to the full gradient history. The failure can occur even along bounded iterates. Our example is inspired by the one of Parshakova et al. which only covers $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2})$. Then, we show that the obstruction lies in fixed momentum rather than orthogonalization. Indeed, when the momentum factor is adaptive and approaches 1 together with a vanishing step size, Muon recovers asymptotic convergence for nonconvex nonsmooth optimization under the boundedness and regularity conditions. Moreover, we propose MAGD, which combines orthogonalized momentum with gradient, weighted based on their relative progress. MAGD retains asymptotic convergence in nonconvex settings and achieves an $O(\min\{m,n\}ε^{-2})$ rate in convex settings. A lower bound shows the optimal dimension dependence. Experiments on synthetic problems, image classification, and LLM pretraining show MAGD is a simple and practical alternative to Muon. Together, our results characterize when orthogonalized momentum fails without smoothness and how it can be made reliable and we hope that the analysis may be useful more broadly.

title: Achieving perfect completeness for one- and two-message quantum proof systems
comments: 27 pages, 1 figure, 3 protocols. v3: Added an alternative proof of QCMA=QCMA_1, additional related work, and minor changes. v2: A simplified construction of QMA=QMA_1, along with minor changes
summary:
While quantum interactive proof systems using at least three messages can achieve perfect completeness, as shown by Kitaev and Watrous (STOC 2000), whether perfect completeness is achievable for one- and two-message quantum proof systems has remained open. For the one-message case, whether $\sf QMA$ can achieve perfect completeness was posed as an open problem in Watrous (FOCS 2000) and Aharonov and Naveh (2002); for the two-message case, the corresponding problems were (implicitly) posed in Jain, Upadhyay, and Watrous~(FOCS 2009) and Kobayashi, Le Gall, and Nishimura (SICOMP, 2019).
  In this work, we establish that ${\sf QIP}(2)$, ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$, $\sf QAM$, and $\sf QMA$ can achieve perfect completeness. Here ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$ denotes the class of promise problems admitting two-message quantum-public-coin quantum interactive proof systems in which the verifier's only message consists of half-EPR pairs. Our main technical contributions are the follows:
  1. For $\sf QMA$ (and directly for $\sf QAM$), an exactly constructible block-encoded matrix whose kernel certifies yes instances, constructed from the acceptance operator induced by the verification circuit. This also yields an alternative proof of ${\sf QCMA}={\sf QCMA}_1$.
  2. For ${\sf QIP}(2)$ (and implicitly ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$), a new turn-halving transformation that preserves completeness and ensures that the resulting proof system retains at least two messages, provided that the terminal state before the final measurement is efficiently preparable.
comment: 27 pages, 1 figure, 3 protocols. v3: Added an alternative proof of QCMA=QCMA_1, additional related work, and minor changes. v2: A simplified construction of QMA=QMA_1, along with minor changes

title: Encoder Awakening via Adapters: Effective Domain-Adaptive Fine-tuning of Speech-LLMs
comments: Camera ready for IEEE SLT 2026 (figure1 revised)
summary: Speech Large Language Models (Speech-LLMs), typically built from a pre-trained speech encoder, a modality projector, and an LLM fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA), have shown strong Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) performance on general-domain speech. However, adapting them to domain-shifted speech, such as child or dialectal speech, remains challenging under limited target-domain data. Given the dominant role of the LLM in Speech-LLMs, with cross-entropy loss applied only at the LLM output, the speech encoder may receive insufficient adaptation to new acoustic conditions. In this paper, we propose Encoder Awakening via Adapters (EAVA), a simple yet effective domain-adaptive fine-tuning method for Speech-LLM-based ASR. First, lightweight adapters are inserted into each encoder layer and trained exclusively, enabling target-domain acoustic knowledge to be incorporated into the encoder while preserving its pre-trained knowledge. Second, the full model is jointly fine-tuned on the target domain with LoRA applied to the LLM. Experiments on three domain-shifted ASR datasets, covering child and dialectal speech, show that EAVA consistently outperforms vanilla fine-tuning and other baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art performance.
comment: Camera ready for IEEE SLT 2026 (figure1 revised)

title: From Optimal Transport to Optimal Quantization: A Variational Study of the Witsenhausen Counterexample
summary: Witsenhausen's counterexample is a canonical problem in decentralized control: a two-stage linear-quadratic-Gaussian team problem in which nonlinear policies strictly outperform every affine one. This paper develops a variational and computational framework for the scalar counterexample based on optimal transport. Building on the transport formulation of Wu and Verdú, we absorb the first controller into a transport map and recast the problem as $J^\star=\inf_Q\{k^2W_2^2(P,Q)+\mathrm{mmse}(Q)\}$, which trades a quadratic Wasserstein transport cost against a minimum mean-square estimation error. The optimal first controller is the monotone rearrangement that pushes the prior $P$ to a minimizer $Q^\star$. We establish the existence and absolute continuity of minimizers, derive an Euler--Lagrange optimality condition, and obtain a semi-closed-form Gaussian benchmark with an explicit second-variation stability threshold. We then show that restricting to finitely supported laws yields an MMSE-regularized optimal quantizer: its optimal values decrease to $J^\star$, its weak limit points are minimizers of the continuous problem, and its stationarity conditions pair centroid levels with power cells, recovering Lloyd--Max quantization as control becomes expensive. This structure leads to an estimation-aware Lloyd algorithm with signalling-based initialization. As $k\to\infty$, the optimal controllers converge to the classical affine pair; as $k\to0$, $J^\star(k)=σ^2k^2+o(k^2)$ and the optimal laws collapse onto $δ_0$, so signalling constellations are a moderate-$k$ phenomenon. Numerical experiments corroborate the theory, and the framework extends to the vector counterexample, where the finite-level program becomes an MMSE-regularized vector quantizer.

title: Robust LassoNet: Enhancing Feature Selection in Neural Networks via Robust Loss Functions
summary: Feature selection in neural networks remains a challenging problem, particularly in the presence of noisy or contaminated data. LassoNet is a recent approach that addresses this issue by combining neural networks with hierarchical sparsity constraints, enabling simultaneous prediction and variable selection. However, its standard formulation relies on the mean squared error (MSE) loss, which is known to be highly sensitive to outliers. In this paper, we present Robust LassoNet, an extension of LassoNet that incorporates robust loss functions, such as Huber, Cauchy, Tukey's bisquare, and Nonnegative Garrote, to mitigate the effect of extreme observations. The proposed approach preserves the original optimization framework while improving stability under data contamination. Through experiments on synthetic and real datasets, we show that robust LassoNet significantly improves both predictive performance and feature selection accuracy in the presence of outliers or heavy tailed noise, while maintaining comparable performance in clean settings. These results highlight the importance of robustness in neural network based feature selection and suggest practical guidelines for choosing appropriate loss functions.

title: Near-Minimax-Optimal Rates for Asynchronous TD Learning with Markovian Data
summary: We study the last iterate of standard importance-weighted temporal-difference (TD) learning from a single trajectory of a finite Markov decision process. The trajectory follows a behavior policy $b$ with an irreducible, possibly periodic state chain; a target policy $π$ covered by $b$ is evaluated with action importance ratios bounded by $\varrho$. Write $H=(1-γ)^{-1}$, with $μ_{\min}$ the minimum stationary probability and $\mathfrak h_\star$ the largest expected hitting time of the reverse behavior state chain. We prove that the last iterate achieves sup-norm error at most $\varepsilon$ with high probability after $\widetilde O(\varrho H^3/(μ_{\min}\varepsilon^2)+\mathfrak h_\star)$ transitions for $0<\varepsilon\le1$. The statistical term retains the cubic effective-horizon dependence of synchronous TD, while the initialization cost is additive in $\mathfrak h_\star$. Setting $b=π$ and $\varrho=1$ recovers the on-policy rate. For aperiodic behavior chains, $\mathfrak h_\star=\widetilde O(t_{\rm mix}/μ_{\min})$ recovers a mixing-time bound. The proof combines an anchored local Poisson equation in reverse time to control fluctuations without a mixing-time factor, a compensation argument for successive hitting costs, and an expected cumulative propagation mass bound for decreasing step sizes. Given the policy ratios and their bound, an empirical state-count rule attains the same rate without prior knowledge of model parameters. The framework covers nonnegative affine importance-weighted prediction updates, including successor features, transition-dependent discounting, and coupled finite-mode predictions. A perturbation estimate yields a time-uniform guarantee for online return-variance estimation. A three-state, two-action construction gives matching minimax lower bounds for both terms up to logarithmic factors on the considered parameter classes.

title: Hamiltonian locality testing and certification do not achieve the Heisenberg limit
summary:
We establish lower bounds for Hamiltonian property testing with access to the time-evolution operator but not its inverse. Each experiment may query the time-evolution operator multiple times, and distances between Hamiltonians are measured in the normalized Frobenius norm.
  In this model, we show that testing whether a Hamiltonian is $k$-local or $\varepsilon$-far from every $k$-local Hamiltonian requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Kallaugher and Liang (TQC'25). We also prove that testing whether an unknown Hamiltonian equals a target Hamiltonian or is $\varepsilon$-far from it requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Sinha and Tong (2025). These are the first lower bounds for natural problems in Hamiltonian learning and testing that rule out Heisenberg-limited scaling of $1/\varepsilon$.
  As a third result, we show that amplitude estimation to precision $\varepsilon$ requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total time evolution, recovering the result of Tang and Wright (QIP'26) in the continuous-time query model. All three results follow from the hardness of distinguishing the zero Hamiltonian from a suitably chosen ensemble of random Hamiltonians. We establish this hardness by adapting the continuous-time adversary method to forward Hamiltonian evolution.

title: Explicit Asymptotic Bounds for Sequential Calibration Beyond $T^{2/3}$
summary:
Probability forecasts are calibrated when predicted probabilities match empirical outcome frequencies: among events assigned a probability $p$, we'd hope that the fraction of positive outcomes is close to $p$. We study the problem of sequential forecasting of binary outcomes. The classical $O(T^{2/3})$ bound on expected cumulative $\ell_1$-calibration error established by Foster and Vohra stood for over two decades until Dagan et al. reduced the exponent $2/3$ by an unspecified constant.
  We establish a new two-phase recursive labeling strategy for the sign-preservation-with-reuse game that yields the bound $O(n^αt^β)$ for all choices of space and time. We then sharpen the reduction from upper bounds on sign preservation to calibration by modifying the equivalence of Dagan et al. to use only $O(\log T)$ instances of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game. This lets us establish an explicit bound of $O(T^{0.662942288})$, the first explicit exponent below $2/3$ for sequential calibration, by combining both improvements and choosing explicit feasible parameters.

title: When Does Interference Help Learning? Kernel Geometry as a Pre-Experimental Test for Photonic Reservoir Computing
summary: Multi-photon interference is the resource most native to photonic quantum machine learning, yet experiments on photonic reservoirs have reported advantages, null results, and train-only effects. These outcomes cannot be compared: each measures task-dependent accuracy on different tasks and platforms. Here we resolve the question task-independently through the kernel geometry of boson-sampling feature maps. Interference redistributes feature variance across roughly twice as many effective dimensions as distinguishable-particle statistics, generating a large geometric separation between the corresponding kernels. The separation grows superlinearly with indistinguishability, is linear in Hong--Ou--Mandel visibility at small visibility for two to four photons, and retains approximately 80% of its magnitude at the source quality of current quantum processors. Under experimental sampling budgets the separation is learnable on adversarially constructed tasks (accuracy advantage +0.22 plus or minus 0.05) and an order of magnitude smaller on natural tasks, gated by kernel--task alignment. The results reconcile the existing experimental record and supply a pre-experimental protocol: kernel geometry establishes that an interference-specific learning resource exists, and task alignment determines whether a given task can access it; both are computable before committing significant hardware resources.

title: Beyond QAOA: A Review of AI and Quantum Computing for Adaptive Combinatorial Optimization
comments: 36 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables; supplementary evidence matrix included as ancillary file. v2: clarified terminologies, co-optimization definition and evidence denominators; added references, minor corrections
summary: Near-term quantum approaches to combinatorial optimization are limited by qubit counts, circuit fidelity, sampling cost, and the difficulty of encoding constraints, while machine learning is increasingly used to configure and control quantum optimization workflows. We call such workflows adaptive: decisions conventionally fixed in advance, from formulation and penalties to shot budgets, backends, and whether to invoke a quantum processor at all, are made by learned policies that respond to the instance, the progress of the solve, or the hardware. This review examines three paradigms, AI for quantum optimization, quantum for AI-driven optimization, and AI-quantum co-optimization, and organizes the literature by the decision being learned rather than by application. A structured search identified a 119-paper corpus, of which 67 papers form an evidence core coded in detail. The evidence is considerably stronger for AI-assisted quantum optimization than for the reverse direction: learning already reduces quantum evaluations, improves initialization, supports decomposition and penalty control, and mitigates noise, whereas evidence that quantum computation improves learned optimizers remains largely confined to small-scale simulation. Experimental controls are thin: of 52 studies in the three paradigms, 22 include no classical baseline, the quantum contribution is fully isolated in 10 of 24 where an ablation applies, and the median largest experiment uses 16 qubits. We introduce an M0-M5 evidence hierarchy, from simulation to practical quantum advantage, and find no broadly convincing result at the highest level. We argue that scaling is increasingly a systems problem: the question is not only whether a problem fits on a quantum processor, but how classical and quantum resources should be allocated across the optimization process.

title: Efficient quadratic entropy with distance sketches
comments: Code for reproducing results in LaTeX comments; removed submission checklist from v1
summary: We detail scalable methods for approximating the quadratic entropy $p^T d p$ for arbitrary distributions $p$ and common distances $d$ of negative type. We focus on the Euclidean and spherical geodesic cases, which both use random feature embeddings and projections to dramatically improve computational complexity within a simple framework. Amortization of a single large matrix multiplication and control variates further enable computation at large scale with low memory and runtime in situations where $d$ is held constant while $p$ varies. We demonstrate this with a comparison against direct pair sampling and bibliometric/scientometric examples on Open Graph Benchmark datasets, revealing papers, fields, and institutions with both particularly narrow and broad interdisciplinary reach from their citations and text features alone.

title: Ultrasound and Magnetic Resonance Elastography of the Neck: Biomechanical Basis, Clinical Applications and Methodological Challenges
summary: Many neck disorders, from chronic neck pain and headache to thyroid and nodal malignancy and radiation-induced fibrosis, both arise from and alter the mechanical properties of neck tissues, yet clinical assessment still relies on morphology, palpation and symptoms. Ultrasound and magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) now allow these properties to be measured in vivo, but the neck literature differs widely in methodology and remains dispersed across modalities and tissues. This review brings together the biomechanical basis of neck tissue behavior, the clinical conditions that alter it, and the principles and applications of ultrasound elastography and MRE in the neck. We show that ultrasound elastography has demonstrated diagnostic value for thyroid nodules and cervical lymph nodes, while neck MRE has been shown to be feasible but remains at an early stage. Across both modalities, reported values depend strongly on fiber orientation, posture, muscle activation and acquisition conditions. We therefore propose reporting recommendations and discuss how measurements beyond stiffness, including anisotropy, viscosity and nonlinearity, could improve disease management and inform computational models of the neck.

title: On the Performance of Randomly Generated Codebooks in Near-Field Communications
summary: Near-field communication with large antenna arrays requires beamforming techniques that account for spherical wavefront effects. While predefined codebooks are widely used in multiple-antenna wireless systems, the performance of randomly generated codebooks in the near-field region has not been investigated. In this work, we study four randomly generated codebooks for near-field communications: random vector quantization (RVQ), random phase (RP), random far-field (RFF), and random near-field (RNF) codebooks. We use the known RVQ gain distribution as a benchmark. For RP, we derive a large-array bulk approximation and characterize the high-gain tail behavior of the gain distribution. For RNF, we characterize the high-gain tail behavior of the gain distribution. For RFF, we derive an analytical approximation for the maximum achievable beamforming gain when far-field beams are used to serve near-field users, along with the corresponding maximizing far-field direction. We also analyze the maximum-gain scaling with codebook size. Monte Carlo simulations verify the analytical results and show that RVQ and RP degrade significantly as the array size increases, while RNF achieves the most favorable high-gain scaling. RFF can outperform RVQ and RP for finite codebook sizes, but its maximum gain saturates below one due to the phase mismatch between the far-field beams and the near-field channel. These results show how codebook structure, array size, and codebook size affect random beamforming performance in the near-field.

title: Simultaneous Direct and Indirect Channel Estimation for RIS-Assisted MIMO Communications
summary: This paper introduces an enhanced channel estimation method for reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications. Considering the presence of both the direct link from the base station (BS) to the user equipment (UE) and the indirect link \textit{via} the RIS, we formulate a tensor-based receiver for joint direct and indirect channel estimation called the TenDICE algorithm. The proposed receiver relies on an extended parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC) tensor model for the received pilot signals, from which the involved (direct and indirect link) channels are estimated using a simple alternating least squares scheme. The proposed TenDICE method is compared with the state-of-the-art least squares (LS) method, Khatri-Rao factorization (KRF) method, enhanced trilinear alternating least squares (E-TALS), and the theoretical Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) based on normalized mean square error (NMSE) and spectral efficiency (SE). The proposed TenDICE outperforms the LS and E-TALS methods and performs similarly to the KRF methods while estimating the direct channel.

title: Low-Complexity Tensor-Based Channel Parameter Estimation for mmWave MIMO-Assisted Systems
summary: This paper presents a low-complexity tensor-based channel estimation framework for downlink mmWave massive MIMO systems using passive Butler-matrix beamforming. By modeling received signals as a third-order PARAFAC tensor, we exploit known pilot structures via bilinear alternating least-squares (BALS) optimization to reduce computational overhead. The decoupled spatial factors are then processed via 1D and 2D ESPRIT to extract angles of arrival and departure with automatic pairing. Additionally, we derive the Cramer--Rao lower bound (CRLB) for this architecture. Simulations confirm the proposed estimator outperforms conventional least-squares, achieving accurate channel reconstruction and approaching the CRLB at moderate-to-high signal-to-noise ratios.

title: Multistatic Terahertz ISAC for Object Shape Identification
comments: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to IEEE GLOBECOM 2026 Workshops (Third Workshop on Positioning and Sensing Over Wireless Networks)
summary: 6G networks are expected to sense their surroundings using the same waveforms that carry data. We ask how much can be learned about the shape of an object from the terahertz echoes that user equipment transmissions produce as they scatter from that object on their way to a ceiling-mounted access point, with no sensing hardware beyond the communication link itself. We build a physics-based multistatic forward model at a 300 GHz carrier with 50 GHz of bandwidth, combining Physical Optics (PO) and Physical Theory of Diffraction (PTD) scattering with an image-source multipath lattice, molecular absorption and directional horn antennas. The model makes explicit a property of the PO mechanism hierarchy that is usually left implicit. Six physically distinct mechanisms share only three frequency exponents, so the spectral slope does not by itself determine which mechanisms a target presents and therefore cannot by itself determine its geometry. Angular diversity is accordingly a requirement for identifiability rather than an optional refinement. We compare a transmitter-count-invariant 2D-CNN with a physics-informed RBF-SVM on object orientations never seen in training. Accuracy climbs from roughly 70 percent with one transmitter to 96-97 percent with 20. The CNN gains in two regimes, irregular placement and lossy targets, while on metal under quasi-uniform placement the SVM baseline is fully competitive. Performance falls off gradually under occlusion, holding 78 percent with three quarters of the surface hidden and 63 percent when the classifier has never seen an occluded target. Multi-object scenes are limited by interference between overlapping returns rather than by angular coverage, so presence detection saturates after roughly four transmitters.
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to IEEE GLOBECOM 2026 Workshops (Third Workshop on Positioning and Sensing Over Wireless Networks)

title: Generative Control of Time-Modulated Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces for Scalable Directional Modulation
summary: Time-modulated intelligent reflecting surfaces (TM-IRS) achieve directional modulation by switching their elements on and off at designed instants and durations, so that an undistorted signal reaches the intended user while appearing scrambled elsewhere. We propose a Flow Matching (FM)-based generative framework that designs these parameters for strong scrambling and reliable reception simultaneously. For orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) signals, we introduce a physics-informed reward that maximizes the time-modulation harmonic energy radiated in the null space of the legitimate-user response, subject to a minimum per-subcarrier signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), without requiring knowledge of adversary directions. Unlike prior generative flow network (GFlowNet) approaches, which assign discretized parameters sequentially, the FM model generates complete continuous configurations jointly, decoupling the generation depth from the number of elements and accelerating training. It also learns a distribution over configurations that can be resampled to vary the scrambling pattern. Numerical results show that, compared with a GFlowNet baseline, the proposed approach reduces the time to training loss near-saturation by $99.4\%$ on average for $3{\times}3$ to $12{\times}12$ surfaces, attains higher final rewards, scales to $80{\times}80$, and confines the low-symbol-error region more tightly around the legitimate user.

title: Self-Calibration DOA Estimation for Moving Dilated Arrays with Gain and Phase Errors
summary: Moving dilated arrays (MDAs) can increase the uniform degrees of freedom (uDOFs) while alleviating mutual coupling, but their performance is susceptible to unknown gain and phase errors (GPEs). To deal with this problem, we investigate self-calibration direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation for MDAs with unknown GPEs. First, multi-position observations are phase aligned to construct an equivalent virtual array with an enlarged aperture. Next, the motion-induced relationships among the GPEs are exploited to establish explicit calibration constraints. By leveraging the orthogonality between the steering vectors and the noise subspace, the joint estimation of the DOAs and GPEs is formulated as a constrained optimization problem. To solve this problem, a two-stage alternating optimization (AO) algorithm is developed. In the first stage, the GPEs are estimated in closed form with the DOAs fixed. In the second stage, the estimated GPEs are used to calibrate the covariance matrix, after which the DOAs are refined using the multiple signal classification (MUSIC) algorithm. To obtain reliable initial estimates, a rotational invariance-like (RIL) initialization method is further developed by exploiting two translated virtual subarrays with identical GPEs. Furthermore, the Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) is derived to characterize the theoretical performance limit of the considered system. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method converges reliably and achieves accurate DOA estimation under different array apertures, numbers of snapshots, GPE levels, and numbers of sources.

title: LLM-Assisted Hierarchical Interference Control for Satellite-Terrestrial Integrated Networks
summary: Time-varying aggregate interference from low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites challenges terrestrial-network (TN) protection, whereas conservative control degrades LEO quality of service (QoS). This letter proposes a hierarchical framework combining geometry-based interference estimation, QoS-constrained power control, adaptive energy detection, large language model (LLM)-assisted candidate ranking, stay-or-switch decisions, and target-band selection, with deterministic verification. The current band is retained only when both spectrum-hole and power-feasibility conditions hold, with periodic reevaluation. Over a 300-s horizon with 0.5-s sampling, the proposed method keeps the aggregate INR from exceeding the $-12.2$~dB threshold and achieves a time-averaged mean LEO-link rate of $320.97$~Mbps with $100\%$ QoS satisfaction. It markedly outperforms power-only and satellite-muting in jointly protecting the TN and preserving LEO QoS.

title: Towards Signal Processing In Networks: Multiplierless Block Transforms in Data Plane
comments: Submitted to the 2027 ICASSP-OJSP track, 9 pages, 4 figures
summary: In this paper, we propose a signal processing concept, signal processing in networks (SPIN), that executes signal processing tasks directly on programmable switches. Traditionally, signal processing tasks, such as denoising, decomposition, and dimensionality reduction, are performed on edge or cloud servers, i.e., raw streams are transmitted from sensors. This imposes a heavy processing load on edge/cloud servers and requires substantial bandwidth. SPIN addresses this problem by performing signal processing on the forwarding path. As an initial realization of SPIN, we implement a DCT-based block transform on a programmable switch. We redesign its computation using a lifting-based lattice structure, multiplierless approximation, and pipeline partitioning across stages in a programmable switch. We verify at the compiler level that the proposed implementation satisfies the strict hardware constraints of the Intel Tofino2--specifically regarding pipeline stages, packet header vector, and ternary content-addressable memory usage--and therefore enables line-rate processing. We further quantify the per-packet latency of the ingress match-action pipeline. The SPIN-oriented preprocessing adds 46 cycles (approximately 31 ns at 1.5 GHz). The total ingress match-action unit latency is approximately 87 ns, which remains consistent with the low-latency operation targeted by SPIN. Furthermore, we implement the proposed block transform on a BMv2 switch using P4 and evaluate it as preprocessing for in-network machine learning. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method improves classification performance over unfiltered baselines.
comment: Submitted to the 2027 ICASSP-OJSP track, 9 pages, 4 figures

title: Scalable Quantum Clustering of Renewable Profiles via a Hybrid Qubit-efficient Strategy
summary: Large-scale renewable energy profile clustering is a computationally challenging NP-hard problem. Recent quantum computing techniques offer a potential remedy, yet their scalability is severely constrained by the limited qubit count of current quantum hardware. To address this issue, we first cast the problem into a QUBO form and then we propose a consensus-based variable reduction (CBVR) method to drastically cut qubit usage. More specifically, we tailor the one-hot constraint to eliminate assignment variables and leverage consensus analysis to convert stable clustering relations from initial anneals into equality constraints for further reduction. Experiments on real quantum hardware confirm that CBVR compresses oversized QUBO models into feasible sizes while retaining high clustering quality and efficiency.

title: Blind and Asynchronous Initial Beam Acquisition and Clock-Assisted Re-Acquisition in Standalone Mobile MIMO-OFDM Systems
summary: Building upon our preliminary study, this paper proposes a standalone beam-management framework for mobile MIMO-OFDM systems that integrates Blind Initial Beam Acquisition (BIBA) with Clock-Assisted Re-Acquisition (CARA). BIBA is a blind and asynchronous protocol that requires neither prior synchronization nor an out-of-band feedback channel, so the Base Station (BS) and User Equipment (UE) can independently identify the beam pair maximizing received signal strength. To handle subsequent link drops, the newly introduced CARA protocol exploits the clock synchronization established after BIBA to reduce the re-acquisition time by approximately 55% compared with BIBA. The operational reliability of both protocols is bounded by a probabilistic feasibility analysis under random UE mobility trajectories. Protocols are validated on a 28 GHz mmWave testbed under practical hardware constraints, including beam-switching and Time Division Duplex (TDD) latencies, and measured Software-Defined Radio (SDR) software processing delays. Finally, we formulate a unified Finite State Machine (FSM) model for both BIBA and CARA to ensure robust integration into practical wireless systems

title: Suppressing Multiple GNSS Interferers with Local-Gradient Adaptive Notch Filtering
summary: Adaptive notch filters (ANFs) based on the normalized least mean squares (NLMS) algorithm are an established technique for suppressing narrowband interference in GNSS receivers. The traditional solution for multiple interferers is simply cascading the NLMS-ANF into multiple stages but this solution degrades performance when multiple chirp jammers of similar power are present. We propose a low-complexity modification to the cascaded NLMS-ANF update rule to resolve this: a local gradient (LG) formulation: LG-ANF. The LG-ANF forms a locally bandlimited gradient signal by translating the input to baseband around the current frequency estimate, low-pass filtering it, and translating it back, thereby attenuating competing interferers before adaptation. The modification generalizes the traditional NLMS-ANF to handle the similar-power multiple interferer problem, using just one additional parameter. We characterize the gradient-averaging failure analytically and visually, demonstrate independent chirp tracking in the worst-case two-chirp scenarios, and evaluate statistical suppression performance by sweeping amplitude ratio against a standard NLMS-ANF, a frequency-locked-loop (FLL)-based ANF and a per-sample oracle upper bound. We further characterize the LG advantage over various ANF parameters and chirp conditions. Simulations show that the LG-ANF reduces to the standard NLMS-ANF outside the pathological multi-chirp regime, while recovering up to 4dB of in-band suppression around pathological amplitude ratios under per-condition optimization of the local bandwidth, and up to 13dB for selected edge-case parameter combinations. These optimized results represent an upper bound on the achievable LG gain. In a hardware experiment using a fixed alpha_lp=0.5, the LG-ANF extends position-lock survival by 24s relative to the standard ANF.

title: HF Single-Station Localization via Multimode Ray Tracing and Time-Frequency Information Fusion
summary: High-frequency (HF) single-station localization estimates an emitter location from measured directions of arrival (DOAs) and an ionospheric propagation model. When the propagation mode composition cannot be identified from conventional direction-finding (DF) measurements, the same DF observation may produce multiple physically valid ground landing points under different propagation modes, making the location inversion ambiguous. This paper proposes a multimode time-frequency information fusion localization method (MTFIF-L).Rather than assuming a propagation mode a priori, MTFIF-L retains valid landing points generated under different propagation modes and uses repeated observations across time windows and, when available, multiple operating frequencies to progressively constrain the resulting candidate locations. Experiments on four measured HF links examine the respective roles of multimode candidate retention, cross-window processing, and cross-frequency processing. All four links yield unique location decisions. Links A--C achieve relative errors of $1.40\%$, $0.78\%$, and $3.41\%$, respectively.Link D, the only single-frequency case, also yields a unique decision from repeated temporal observations, although its post- localization error is substantially larger. Propagation-path analysis further reveals link-dependent differences in reflection layer, hop count, magnetoionic mode, and elevation angle among the ray-tracing paths associated with the measured links.Overall, the results show that repeated temporal observations can support localization within an individual frequency, while multifrequency information provides additional robustness against unreliable frequency-specific outcomes, enabling HF single-station localization under unknown and potentially coexisting propagation modes while retaining interpretable propagation information for post-localization analysis.

title: OpenH-RF: A Large-Scale Ultrasound Raw Channel Dataset Initiative
comments: Preprint: 15 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables. Dataset (v1.0): https://open-h.github.io/OpenH-RF
summary: Medical ultrasound is a widely accessible, real-time imaging modality, yet progress in data-driven ultrasound research is constrained by the scarcity of large, open collections of raw channel data. Existing public datasets are predominantly based on reconstructed images, while the smaller number of open raw channel datasets is generally specialized to individual reconstruction or imaging tasks, limiting the development of general-purpose methods and foundation models that operate directly on ultrasound signals. While interpretive tasks can be performed on reconstructed images, many of the key technical challenges in ultrasound imaging, such as aberration correction and reverberation reduction, require the raw channel data itself. We introduce OpenH-RF, a community-driven open dataset initiative comprising approximately 40 TB of medical ultrasound raw channel data in 19,332 acquisitions, contributed by 38 institutions across academia and industry, spanning in-vivo, phantom, and simulated data. Each dataset is annotated with a number of supported tasks, ranging from generalized reconstruction, speed-of-sound estimation, and aberration correction to blood flow imaging, motion estimation, quantitative ultrasound, and image interpretation. OpenH-RF provides a unified, self-contained data format that captures raw channel data together with the acquisition, probe, metadata, and reconstruction information required for reproducible processing across scanners and acquisition schemes. The corpus is publicly hosted under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license and can be streamed programmatically and selectively at scale. By bringing heterogeneous ultrasound data into a common representation, backed by modern data infrastructure, OpenH-RF lowers the barrier to working with raw channel data and aims to open medical ultrasound research to new communities. See https://open-h.github.io/OpenH-RF.
comment: Preprint: 15 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables. Dataset (v1.0): https://open-h.github.io/OpenH-RF

title: A Miniaturized Wi-Fi HaLow-Based Wireless Imaging Transfer System for Capsule Endoscopy
summary:
Wireless capsule endoscopy is constrained by severe limitations in size, available power, and reliable data transmission through biological tissues. Although recent advances in miniature imaging sensors have improved image quality, the wireless transmission of color images at practical frame rates remains a challenging task under the tight capsule constraints.
  We present the design and the experimental validation of a miniaturized Wireless Imaging Transfer (WIT) system for capsule endoscopy based on a sub-GHz IEEE 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow) wireless link. In addition, a preliminary in-vivo validation of Wi-Fi HaLow communication is reported, showing that a stable through-body wireless link can be established across biological tissues in a clinically relevant porcine model. These in-vivo results provide direct experimental support for the adoption of sub-GHz Wi-Fi HaLow for capsule endoscopy applications.
  Experimental results demonstrate stable wireless image transmission at a resolution of 320x320 pixels, with measured end-to-end data rates above 12 Mbps and a transmission energy efficiency of 20.7 nJ/bit. We also report a detailed power consumption analysis, with a breakdown of the contributions from the imaging sensor, illumination, digital processing, and RF transmission. When all active subsystem contributions are considered, including the camera, digital processing, RF transmission, and illumination at 60% LED brightness, the total power consumption is approximately 477 mW, corresponding to a complete-chain energy consumption of approximately 39.6 nJ/bit. Overall, the measured performance confirms that sub-GHz Wi-Fi HaLow provides a promising trade-off among throughput, robustness, and energy efficiency for wireless imaging in capsule endoscopy.

title: Zeros of the Spectrogram of White Noise with Hermite Windows
summary: We study the zeros of the spectrogram of complex white noise analyzed with Hermite windows of order n, extending the classical Gaussian-window correspondence with Gaussian Analytic Functions to the polyanalytic setting. Using the polyanalytic Bargmann transform, these zeros split into two families according to the sign of the local Jacobian, giving rise to a natural notion of charge, and we show that these zeros are almost surely simple, isolated, and form a translation and rotation-invariant point process. We derive closed-form expressions for the one-point intensity, decomposed by charge, and also for the unsigned, signed, and hybrid two-point intensities. Besides, we prove that unlike the total repulsion observed with a Gaussian window, the Hermite window of order n generates a pair correlation function that converges at the origin to a strictly positive constant depending on n. Finally, we propose a numerical method for detecting spectrogram zeros via the winding number around candidate local minima.

title: Cramer-Rao Bound Analysis of Bistatic ISAC Under Partial Symbol Knowledge and Clutter
comments: 6 pages, 6 figures. To be presented at IEEE GLOBECOMM Workshop on Positioning and Sensing Over Wireless Networks
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems rely on communication waveforms to perform sensing tasks, thus making their sensing performance strongly dependent on the level of communication symbol knowledge available to the sensing receivers. However, the existing literature fails to capture this dependency, often relying on assumptions of full symbol knowledge. In this paper, we present a Cramer Rao bound (CRB) analysis of a bistatic ISAC network with heterogeneous uplink and downlink illumination and structured clutter. We consider different symbol knowledge regimes by modeling unknown communication symbols as nuisance parameters. Assuming a temporal evolution of the communication channel, we derive a correlation aware channel estimator and an expression for the UEs uplink spectral efficiency. Numerical results show the CRB degradation induced by clutter and symbol uncertainty and how this can affect resource allocation policies. We also show the performance gain of our channel estimator over conventional block fading architectures.
