title: Dynamic Heartbeat Modeling with Recurrent Neural Networks and Inverse Gaussian Point Process
summary: Heart rate variability (HRV) analysis is important for the assessment of autonomic cardiovascular regulation. The inverse Gaussian process (IGP) has been widely used for beat-to-beat HRV modeling. However, dynamic estimation of the IGP parameters remains a critical challenge. Conventional parametric approaches such as autoregressive models might be insufficient to capture the nonlinear characteristics of R-R series. In this study, we investigated whether recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can be used for IGP parameter identification and thereby enhance probabilistic modeling of R-R dynamics. Four representative RNN architectures, namely, GRU, LSTM, Structured State Space sequence model (S4), and Mamba, were compared and evaluated using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics. The results demonstrate the possibility of combining RNN with the IGP for beat-wise R-R series modeling. This approach provides a flexible basis for probabilistic HRV modeling and for future incorporation of more complex physiological mechanisms and dynamic conditions.

title: Edge-Assisted Multimodal UAV Localization with Resource-Efficient Compression and Robust Fusion
comments: Accepted and published in IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing. This version incorporates the revisions made during peer review
summary: The unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) will play an important role in the future urban transportation systems. This requires designing robust localization schemes especially for non-cooperative UAVs that do not share any information about their movements. This paper designs a multimodal UAV localization framework which utilizes camera, LiDAR and radar sensing modalities. The underlying data processing and the subsequent inference of the UAV location are distributed among the sensing nodes and the edge server attached to the base station. The proposed UAV localization framework addresses three key challenges. First, the sensing nodes have limited computing and communication resources, and they contain only single modality sensors. Second, the multimodal data differ greatly in the sampling rates, time alignment and the encodings. Third, the changes in the environment and the hardware failures cause the modal data to degrade, or to be completely missing. The proposed localization framework utilizes several data processing modules including a information-bottleneck (IB)-based compression module that extracts the most relevant features from each modality, a time-encoding alignment module that provides the unified representation in a shared latent space, a multimodal fusion module that accounts for the degraded and missing data, and a Mamba-based regression module that predicts the present UAV location. The experiments involving a real-world dataset demonstrate that the proposed framework accurately and reliably obtains the UAV location while outperforming other existing frameworks.
comment: Accepted and published in IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing. This version incorporates the revisions made during peer review

title: Input-Correlated Supervision Noise Limits the Benefits of OTA Training for Learned Receivers
summary: While learned wireless receivers are typically studied using synthetic data, the impact of over-the-air (OTA) measurements for training remains unclear. We conducted a 5.88 GHz measurement campaign with a 5G/6G-like orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system across diverse environments and mobility conditions, and trained a neural channel estimator and a capacity-matched end-to-end neural receiver using mixtures of measured and synthetic data. Increasing the OTA fraction revealed a fundamental asymmetry: measured data consistently improved the end-to-end receiver, whereas the channel estimator peaked at an intermediate fraction and degraded with fully measured training. We identified supervision quality as a key contributor: OTA channel labels are derived from noisy received signals and therefore contain supervision errors correlated with the receiver input, whereas decoded bits validated by a cyclic redundancy check (CRC) provide effectively error-free supervision. Denoising the channel labels mitigated the degradation, and a controlled simulation showed that label noise of equal power degrades the estimator far more when it is correlated with the input. For OTA training, end-to-end receivers thus benefit from fully measured data, whereas channel estimators benefit from moderate OTA fractions but require improved label quality.

title: One-Bin Fourier Challenges for Dimension-Free Reconstruction Certification
comments: The author withdraws this paper because the coded-diffraction implementation claimed in Section 3.3 is not established. The certification procedure requires complex-valued linear Fourier measurements, whereas intensity-only acquisition does not directly provide them. The manuscript does not establish the additional acquisition procedure needed to bridge this gap
summary: Partial-Fourier measurement underlies computational imaging, and its reconstructions increasingly come from iterative or learned solvers whose recovery guarantees are conditional on a signal model, a sampling law, and solver accuracy. None of those guarantees transfers to a particular committed output: it can satisfy every acquired coefficient while remaining badly wrong in the unmeasured nullspace. Native Fourier holdout does not repair this, since a spectrally concentrated error is missed unless its bin is drawn, so uniform worst-case risk needs a number of hidden bins proportional to the dimension. We propose a post-commit acceptance test: secret finite-phase masks turn one fixed Fourier readout into dense randomized residual checks, and a median-of-means threshold handles calibrated readout noise. We prove that errors above $E_{\rm rej}$ are rejected and errors below $E_{\rm acc}$ are accepted with confidence $1-δ$ once $q\ge C(1+Nσ^2/E_{\rm rej})^2\log(1/δ)$, explicitly exposing the one-bin resolution floor $Nσ^2/\sqrt q$; in the zero-noise limit, QPSK gives $4^{-q}$ soundness versus $97.9\%$ minimax false acceptance for a worst-case ordinary-bin error. At a fixed noise-to-threshold ratio, measured screening false acceptance fell from about $21\%$ at 16 checks to $5\%$ at 64; a data-consistent learned nullspace failure with NMSE $0.200$ was rejected by $96.9\%$ of challenge banks while 16 ordinary bins missed it $98.9\%$ of the time; and error statistics at 16 checks stayed stable from 128 through $65{,}536$ dimensions. The test supports solver acceptance, model selection, and stopping certification, with a certified fresh-bank error interval.

title: Memory- and Bandwidth-Efficient SPAD-LiDAR Ranging via Coarse-to-Fine Spline Sketching
summary: This work presents an optimized compression framework for direct time-of-flight (dToF) light detection and ranging (LiDAR), using an accurate, compact timestamp-encoding strategy to address the high data-rate bottleneck from single-photon timing information in single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) arrays. We propose a hardware-friendly timestamp-to-depth framework in which a sparse single-photon encoding strategy, namely coarse-to-fine spline sketches (CFSS), projects photon timestamps into fine-grained, low-dimensional representations, called sketch values. CFSS converts timestamps on-the-fly to sketch values and accumulates them with lower memory consumption, without constructing histograms, thereby saving on-chip/device memory. CFSS's closed-form solution for ToF retrieval ensures iteration-free reconstruction. Compared with the conventional sketched-LiDAR framework, the proposed method retains the same compression ratio in the single-peak case, ranging from hundreds$\times$ to thousands$\times$ depending on the accuracy-complexity trade-off, while improving depth-estimation accuracy. Both synthetic and real datasets are used to validate the performance. The CFSS framework is further extended to two-peak scenarios, enabling recovery of objects obscured by partially occluding camouflage and uniformly scattering semi-transparent media. Firmware implementation is also investigated by clearly separating online hardware processing from offline software workloads.

title: SENSE: Semantic Neural Speech Synthesis from Brain Dynamics via Spatial Graph Encoding
summary: Reconstructing speech from non-invasive brain signals offers a promising pathway for restoring communication in individuals who are cognitively intact but unable to speak. Existing EEG-to-speech approaches formulate this task as acoustic reconstruction, optimizing waveform fidelity while ignoring whether the generated speech preserves high-level semantic content. In this work, we revisit this formulation and argue that EEG signals carry not only acoustic but also semantic information. We identify two key limitations of prior methods: (1) the neglect of spatial relationships between EEG electrodes, and (2) the failure to exploit the semantic structure of the N400 paradigm, where congruent and incongruent trials reflect distinct semantic processing. We propose SENSE(Semantic-EEG Neural Speech SynthEsis), which combines a graph-based EEG encoder over electrode geometry with EEG Semantic Conditioning (ESC), aligning EEG to a pretrained semantic space using only congruent trials. On the N400 dataset, SENSE consistently outperforms prior methods on both acoustic and semantic metrics, and model-internal channel attribution suggests distributed reliance on auditory, sensorimotor, and centro-parietal regions, consistent with known speech-perception neuroscience. In the unseen-subject setting, SENSE trained on only two subjects already surpasses the strongest baseline trained on all eighteen subjects in word error rate, and matches it on acoustic metrics with as few as eight subjects.

title: Benchmarking Adult Addressee Classification Across Child- and Adult-Directed Speech Datasets
summary: In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of classification performance for distinguishing child-directed speech (CDS) from adult-directed speech (ADS) using speech data from corpora containing natural in-lab and in-the-wild CDS and ADS. We establish classification benchmarks for these datasets using self-supervised learning (SSL) representations, along with a range of time-pooled representations that go beyond first- and second-order statistics by incorporating cross-channel covariances in high-dimensional embeddings. In addition, we probe these representations to examine how different pooling methods capture prosodic information using linear probes. Overall, SSL-based representations prove particularly effective, achieving the best performance, while different pooling methods offer complementary advantages for the task.

title: A functional mixed-effects model for the joint analysis of amplitude and phase variations in function-valued traits
summary: Quantitative genetics is the study of continuous traits and the statistical analysis of phenotypic variation, that is, the observable differences in physical traits among individuals within a population. If family relationships between individuals are known, phenotypic variation can be partitioned into genetic and environmental components. Some traits, such as growth trajectories, can be described as a function of a continuous index and are known as function-valued traits. However, function-valued traits from different individuals often vary not only in their shape (amplitude) but also in the speed at which the biological process develops (phase). In this work, we present and compare two approaches to account for amplitude and phase variations in estimating the additive genetic and environmental components. The first one follows from a conventional framework where warping functions remove phase variations, and then the aligned curves are analysed. The second approach adopts the perspective of looking at the aligned curve and the warping function as a joint functional object. In both cases, we propose a functional mixed-effects framework that uses functional principal components as the data-driven basis for genetically correlated data. The proposed procedure is applied to simulations and a real-case study of Tribolium castaneum growth trajectories.

title: Warning of infrastructure deformation anomaly through probabilistic analysis of InSAR observations
summary: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) offers a low-cost, wide-area solution for near continuous infrastructure monitoring. However, translating InSAR observations into automated anomaly warnings remains challenging because displacements are relative, affected by uncertainty, and acquired along line of sight (LOS). We introduced a probabilistic warning framework that accounts for these factors. LOS displacements were modelled through a Gaussian distribution. A limit state function was defined to describe the displacement exceedance, and the time-dependent probability of exceedance was evaluated. Instead of a fixed threshold, warnings were identified through abrupt increases in exceedance probability. The framework was validated using three case studies of quay walls in Amsterdam, providing timely anomaly warnings and issued no warnings for the non-collapse case. Results demonstrate the potential of a probabilistic interpretation of InSAR time series for deformation anomaly warning.

title: Sequential Conformal Calibration under Recursive Selection
summary: Conformal prediction provides finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees that can support decision-making in specific settings. In multistage problems, earlier decisions determine the populations relevant to later calibration. When later scores are refit using earlier calibration results, reusing those cases for ranking need not preserve exchangeability with a surviving test case. We study sequential conformal calibration with a fresh fold at each stage: conditional on earlier folds, the selected fold scores and the surviving test score are exchangeable. This yields finite-sample coverage guarantees for every prefix of the decision sequence. For atomless survivor score distributions, we derive a universal Binomial-thinned Beta chain for the realized coverage process. Its law depends only on fold sizes and target levels, even under predictable refitting, and yields exact coverage slack, abstention probabilities, and calibration-conditional guarantees. We further characterize the tradeoff between freshness and data reuse. For fixed scores, strict-survivor reuse is exactly valid. For adaptive scores refit using past calibration data, reusing survivors can incur worst-case rank loss, while blocked designs provide an intermediate option between full reuse and stagewise fresh folds. As a case study, we apply the framework to serial multi-echelon inventory problem and propose a sequential conditional-quantile formulation. Each stock level is learned as a context-dependent quantile of cumulative demand among scenarios satisfying earlier no-backlog constraints. We connect these targets to common-shift stationarity and derive decision-level implications for the resulting calibrated policies. In a three-echelon simulation, fresh-fold refitting achieves 81.98% final-prefix coverage against an 81.82% target while reducing mean cost by 5.5% relative to the Bonferroni baseline.

title: Design-based effect sizes and their synthesis in randomized multiple-baseline experiments
summary: Effect sizes for single-case experimental designs usually rely on models for the baseline trend and the serial dependence, which are challenging to check with few sessions. We develop design-based effect sizes for multiple-baseline experiments with a randomized intervention onset. We define case-level and pooled standardized effects with potential outcomes and propose weighted estimators that are unbiased or asymptotically unbiased without an outcome model. The usual difference between phase means is generally biased when the untreated outcome changes over sessions. For research synthesis, we provide variance estimators and asymptotic confidence intervals that require no model for serial dependence, and variance formulas for planning. Simulations and three randomized studies of reading and writing interventions illustrate the methods.

title: Realized Tail-Risk Conditional Autoregressive Expectile Models: Accurate and Stable Forecasting Performance
summary: A realized tail-risk conditional autoregressive expectile (RTCARE) model is proposed for joint forecasting of value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES). Realized tail measures such as the realized quantile and the realized ES, constructed from intraday high-frequency returns, are incorporated into the dynamics and measurement equations of the conditional expectile, allowing information about lower-tail risk to enter the forecasts. The parameters are estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo, and we evaluate the resulting VaR-ES forecasts in numerical examples and in an empirical application using U.S. stock-return data. Across the considered tail levels, the RTCARE models deliver competitive and often superior forecasting performance relative to existing alternatives, with stable results across Monte Carlo replications and rolling forecast evaluations.

title: Neural posterior inference with state-space models for calibrating ice sheet simulators
summary: Ice sheet models are routinely used to quantify and project an ice sheet's contribution to sea level rise. In order for an ice sheet model to generate realistic projections, its parameters must first be calibrated using observational data; this is challenging due to the nonlinearity of the model equations, the high dimensionality of the underlying parameters, and limited data availability for validation. This study leverages the emerging field of neural posterior approximation for efficiently calibrating ice sheet model parameters and boundary conditions. We make use of a one-dimensional (flowline) Shallow-Shelf Approximation model in a state-space framework. A neural network is trained to infer the underlying parameters, namely the bedrock elevation and basal friction coefficient along the flowline, based on observations of ice velocity and ice surface elevation. Samples from the approximate posterior distribution of the parameters are then used within an ensemble Kalman filter to infer latent model states, namely the ice thickness along the flowline. We show through a simulation study that our approach yields more accurate estimates of the parameters and states than a state-augmented ensemble Kalman filter, which is the current state-of-the-art. We apply our approach to infer the bed elevation and basal friction along a flowline in Thwaites Glacier, Antarctica.

title: Where should the null live? Surrogate tests for clustering of threshold-derived air-quality indices, with application to PM2.5 exceedances in Chile
summary: Air-quality and climate monitoring routinely convert native-resolution measurements into exceedance counts before testing whether high values cluster in time. A surrogate null can be imposed on the derived index or on the native series and then propagated through the same thresholding and aggregation. We show that the two placements can encode different scientific hypotheses and lead to opposite conclusions. In 31 Chilean PM2.5 monitoring stations (2018--2025), weekly clustering of days above the 50 ug m^-3 national 24-hour standard was significant at all stations under an index-level IAAFT null but at only two under a daily native-resolution null; a native generative null with seasonal marginals and short-memory Gaussian-copula dependence agreed with the native surrogate at 30 of 31 stations. Across thresholds spanning the WHO guideline (15 ug m^-3) to the Chilean episode-alert level (80 ug m^-3), index-only rejections increased from 8 of 31 to all eligible stations as monthly event probabilities became more seasonally concentrated, and equalizing monthly event probabilities at the 50 ug m^-3 level reduced index-only decisions from 29 to five. We formalize the issue as null transport through a lossy observation map: an exact aggregate-level equivalent of a native null exists if and only if the randomization kernel is lumpable with respect to that map. A within-fiber diagnostic, which perturbs native amplitudes while keeping the observed index exactly fixed, shows that this condition fails in the monitoring data: the native null distribution moved by a median of 18 times its Monte Carlo variability. Weekly clustering of PM2.5 exceedances in Chile is therefore fully compatible with seasonality plus short-memory daily persistence, and index-level surrogate rejections should not be read as evidence about daily concentration dynamics.

title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO
comments: 115 pages, 6 figures; adds a supplemental appendix on non-Gaussian errors
summary: Estimating the first stage of an instrumental variables (IV) model with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary of technical instruments and a penalty level. First-order asymptotic theory offers no guidance on these choices, as any consistent implementation yields a structural parameter estimator with the same limiting distribution. In finite samples, however, these choices can have a substantial impact on the resulting structural parameter estimate. Working in a model with a single endogenous regressor and homoskedastic Gaussian errors, we use first- and second-order Stein identities to derive the approximate mean squared error (AMSE) of the instrumental-variables LASSO (IV-LASSO) estimator, which can be consistently estimated and used to rank a prespecified list of dictionary-penalty candidates. The AMSE reveals a bias-variance trade-off: more complex first-stage fits better approximate the conditional mean of the endogenous variable but are also more correlated with the structural errors, with complexity measured by the degrees of freedom of the LASSO fit. The weight on this bias rises with the endogeneity of the regressor, a quantity that neither plug-in nor cross-validation penalty rules take into account. Despite the AMSE being derived in a Gaussian model, penalty selection by minimizing the feasible AMSE criterion delivers up to a one-third lower mean squared error compared to cross-validation and plug-in penalty rules in Gaussian and non-Gaussian simulation designs calibrated to the data of Gilchrist and Sands (2016).
comment: 115 pages, 6 figures; adds a supplemental appendix on non-Gaussian errors

title: bayprior: Structured Bayesian Prior Elicitation, Conflict Diagnostics, and Regulatory Reporting
summary: Bayesian clinical trials require a well-specified prior distribution, and regulators increasingly expect that specification to be documented, diagnosed for prior-data conflict, and shown to be robust to reasonable alternatives, yet few R tools connect the full workflow of prior construction, validation, and regulatory justification into a single package. We introduce bayprior, an R package and Shiny application that implements structured expert elicitation via quantile matching, moment matching, and the SHELF roulette method across six distribution families; linear and logarithmic expert opinion pooling with Bhattacharyya agreement diagnostics; derivation of meta-analytic-predictive (MAP) priors from historical trial data via random-effects meta-analysis; prior-data conflict assessment using the Box p-value, S-value (surprisal) surprise index, information divergence, Bhattacharyya overlap, and multivariate Mahalanobis distance; hyperparameter sensitivity analysis with tornado and influence heatmap visualisations; and robust, sceptical, and power prior alternatives. A regulatory reporting module generates self-contained HTML, PDF, or Word documents addressing expectations in the FDA's 2026 draft Bayesian methods guidance and in EMA guidance on incorporating external and historical information. The package is demonstrated on a synthetic oncology Phase II trial. bayprior is available on CRAN and includes a fully modular Shiny application for interactive use.

title: Restricted Entropic and Quadratic Hedging in the Small-Risk-Aversion Limit
summary: In incomplete markets, contingent claims cannot in general be replicated exactly, and hedging must therefore be formulated as an optimization problem over admissible trading strategies. This paper studies the relation between quadratic hedging and entropic hedging in a discrete-time incomplete market when strategies are restricted to bounded finite-dimensional parametric classes. These restrictions induce admissible gain sets that are compact and convex in \(L^2\), providing a common well-posed setting for both the restricted mean-square hedging problem and the restricted exponential-utility hedging problem. The main contribution is to establish a uniform small-risk-aversion expansion of the entropic risk functional over the restricted gain set and to use this uniformity to obtain convergence of the corresponding minimizers. Under a uniform exponential integrability assumption, the restricted entropic hedging gains converge in \(L^2\) to the unique restricted quadratic hedge as the risk-aversion parameter tends to zero. The theoretical result is illustrated numerically in a regularized discrete-time stochastic volatility model of Heston type.

title: Three options are roughly enough - Variance-optimal semi-static hedging in the rough Heston model
summary: This paper studies semi-static variance-optimal hedging of variance swaps in the rough Heston model under a risk-neutral measure. We combine dynamic trading in the underlying asset with static positions in a finite basket of European options, with the aim of minimizing the variance of the residual hedging error. Exploiting the Markovian lift provided by the forward variance curve, the Fourier representations of the claims and the Laplace transform characterization of the log-price, we derive semi-explicit formulas for the optimal strategies and the hedging error. We then study the optimal claim selection problem, investigating numerically how the choice of static instruments depends on the Hurst index. Under standard parametrization, we discover that "three options are roughly enough", i.e. adding three static vanilla options reduces the hedging error by more than 95% relative to the purely dynamic hedge for all considered roughness regimes H= 0.1, 0.3, 0.5.
